content.title: Rulings on Discounts and Shopping During Puja
content.subtitle: Commercial gain vs. Shariah limits on Shirk.
content.body:
As Durga Puja approaches, advertisements begin appearing everywhere—from city streets to social media feeds—offering deals such as “Sharadiya Dhamaka,” “Puja Special Offer,” and various special discounts. When a Muslim business owner uses a polytheistic religious festival as an occasion to promote and sell their products simply to attract customers or increase profits, they may think, “It is just business!” But have we ever stopped to consider: by increasing our sales, whose festival are we helping glorify, and whose displeasure are we inviting?

A Clear Prohibition Against Supporting Sin

Earning profit through business is permissible in Islam. However, when an income involves the direct or indirect promotion of a grave sin such as Shirk, it can never be the ideal conduct of a believer. Allah Almighty clearly commands in the Quran:

“Cooperate with one another in righteousness and piety, and do not cooperate in sin and transgression...” (Surah Al-Ma’idah, 5:2)

Using a non-Muslim religious festival as an occasion for special “Puja Offers” or discount campaigns essentially contributes to promoting and normalizing that religious festival. Promoting one’s business around something that incurs the displeasure of Allah clearly falls under cooperating in sinful acts.

The Fiqh Perspective and a Serious Warning

The world-renowned fatwa body Al-Lajnah Ad-Da’imah states unequivocally that assisting in the religious festivals of non-Muslims, promoting them through the media, or offering commercial discounts and financial gifts specifically for their festivals is not permissible for a Muslim. [Fatawa Al-Lajnah Ad-Da’imah, 26/409]

Imam Ibn Nujaym (RA) and classical works of Islamic jurisprudence contain stern warnings regarding honoring non-Muslims’ religious festivals by giving gifts or intending to elevate the significance of such occasions. [Al-Bahr ar-Ra’iq, 5/133; Fath al-Bari, 2/315]

Using a festival disliked by Allah as an advertising slogan simply for the sake of worldly profit is fundamentally inconsistent with a believer’s sense of faith and dignity.

Ordinary Shopping vs. Accepting a Puja Discount

If offering discounts specifically for Puja is impermissible for a business owner, a natural question arises for ordinary customers: If someone else offers such a discount, can a Muslim purchase products from that store?

The basic principle of Shariah is that even if a shop offers a discount on the occasion of Puja, purchasing ordinary halal and necessary products from that shop does not automatically become impermissible. The buying and selling of halal products is fundamentally permissible, and purchasing something at a lower price is not the same as emotionally identifying with or endorsing the religious festival. However, one must never intend to honor the festival or participate in it.

A Moment of Self-Reflection and What Believers Should Do

If business owners want to increase sales during this period, they can offer discounts without associating them with any religious festival—for example, by calling them an “October Offer” or a “Seasonal Discount.”

Yet, an even more painful reality is that during Muslim religious occasions such as Eid-ul-Fitr or Adha, product prices in our country often rise sharply, while an unhealthy competition to offer discounts emerges during non-Muslim religious festivals. Such a mindset raises serious questions about a believer’s sense of dignity and religious identity.

Let us not allow calculations of worldly profit and loss to overturn our calculations for the Hereafter. For the sake of a few additional sales, we should never place a slogan on our shop or business that may invite the displeasure of the One who is the sole Owner and Master of the heavens and the earth. Let us place our complete trust in the One who provides our sustenance and keep our businesses and earnings completely free from every form of association with Shirk.

Answered by: Mufti Muhammad Khairul Islam (Hafizahullah)
